data.title: Atomicity
data.tagline: The property that related operations either all take effect or none of them does
data.learningOutcome: You can identify a check and update that must be indivisible and verify only one successful result.
data.description: When two people buy the last item at the same time, checking and deducting inventory must be an indivisible whole so one succeeds and the other fails. Atomicity covers only the defined operation scope; it does not make every distributed step across systems roll back together.

learning.assumes: You know that multiple requests can change the same data at once.
learning.outcome: You can identify a check and update that must be indivisible and verify only one successful result.

distinctions.label: Transaction
distinctions.explanation: Atomicity emphasizes that operations cannot be split and intermediate states are never exposed; a Transaction is the database container mechanism providing atomicity and isolation.

distinctions.label: Lock
distinctions.explanation: A Lock is a mutual-exclusion mechanism for concurrent access; Atomicity is the indivisible guarantee of the final result.

explanation.title: Problem and key mechanism
explanation.text: When two requests read the last item separately from deducting it, both may believe they can succeed; make the check and deduction one indivisible action so only the request that still meets the condition decrements stock and the other fails as a whole.

explanation.title: How to observe the improvement
explanation.text: The other request should fail completely with an out-of-stock response, without producing a second successful order. Then verify that remaining inventory, the successful order count, and the failure feedback all agree.

explanation.title: Claiming a support ticket also needs atomicity
explanation.text: When two agents claim the same ticket, checking that it is unassigned and assigning the owner must be one atomic operation. Only one agent succeeds; the other is told it was already claimed.

data.boundary: Atomicity covers only the defined scope of operations. It does not mean payment, shipping, or other distributed services across systems can roll back as one unit.

lessonPractice.title: There is only 1 item in stock, and two requests both read 1. Which change keeps the result correct?

options.label: Combine the inventory condition check and deduction into one indivisible database operation
options.feedback: Correct. Only a request that passes the check completes the deduction; the other fails clearly instead of creating a second sale.

options.label: Let both requests read inventory first, then have each write inventory minus one
options.feedback: Both requests can write based on the stale value, producing two orders or an incorrect inventory result.

options.label: Disable the button on both users' pages and wait for one request to finish
options.feedback: A page button state cannot restrict another user or a retry; concurrency protection must be enforced where the shared data is updated.

data.agentPrompt: Inspect the purchase flow: when inventory is 1, simulate two concurrent requests and make the inventory check and deduction one indivisible database operation. Verify that exactly one order succeeds, inventory becomes 0, and the other request receives out-of-stock; do not treat a disabled frontend button as concurrency protection.
